issues.legal_issue: A transfer of a debtor’s property made for adequate consideration to discharge genuine debts is not voidable merely because some creditors are paid while another remains unpaid, where the debtor retains no benefit.
material_facts: The company transferred its assets and used the sale proceeds to pay genuine debts owed to its creditors.
The tax claim remained unpaid after the proceeds were distributed.
The High Court found that the consideration was not inadequate and that the proceeds were used to pay the company’s creditors.
issues.conclusion: The transfer was not voidable under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act merely because the tax creditor remained unpaid after other creditors were paid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act makes a transfer intended to defeat or delay creditors voidable, but preferring one creditor over another is not by itself fraudulent if the transfer is for adequate consideration in satisfaction of genuine debts and the debtor retains no benefit. The Court relied on Musahar Sahu v. Hakim Lal, In re Moroney, Middleton v. Pollock, and MA PWA MAY v. S.R.M.M.A. Chettyar Firm.

rule.if: creditor_transfer_challenge and genuine_debts_paid and adequate_consideration and debtor_retained_no_benefit

predicates.creditor_transfer_challenge: A creditor challenges a debtor’s transfer of property on the ground that it defeats or delays creditors.
predicates.genuine_debts_paid: The transfer proceeds are applied to discharge genuine debts owed by the debtor.
predicates.adequate_consideration: The debtor receives consideration that is not inadequate for the transferred property.
predicates.debtor_retained_no_benefit: The debtor does not reserve or retain a benefit in the transferred property or its proceeds.
predicates.transfer_not_voidable_merely_for_prefere: The transfer is not voidable merely because some creditors are paid while another creditor remains unpaid.

issues.definition: When a creditor challenges a property transfer, payment of genuine debts for adequate consideration without a retained benefit means that the transfer is not voidable merely because it prefers some creditors.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer to a person who is not a creditor is not invalid merely because the transferee is not a creditor when the transfer is for adequate consideration and its proceeds discharge genuine debts without a benefit being retained by the debtor.
material_facts: The company transferred its assets to a firm that was not itself a creditor.
The High Court found that the sale was made to discharge the company’s debts, that the proceeds were used to pay creditors, and that the consideration was not inadequate.
issues.conclusion: The transferee’s status as a non-creditor did not make the transfer voidable under section 53 on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act, a transfer made for adequate consideration to pay genuine debts, without the debtor retaining a benefit, is not impeachable merely because the transferee is not a creditor. This follows the principle in Musahar Sahu v. Hakim Lal, In re Moroney, Middleton v. Pollock, and MA PWA MAY v. S.R.M.M.A. Chettyar Firm.

rule.if: creditor_transfer_challenge and genuine_debts_paid and adequate_consideration and debtor_retained_no_benefit and transferee_not_creditor

predicates.creditor_transfer_challenge: A creditor challenges a debtor’s transfer of property on the ground that it defeats or delays creditors.
predicates.genuine_debts_paid: The transfer proceeds are applied to discharge genuine debts owed by the debtor.
predicates.adequate_consideration: The debtor receives consideration that is not inadequate for the transferred property.
predicates.debtor_retained_no_benefit: The debtor does not reserve or retain a benefit in the transferred property or its proceeds.
predicates.transferee_not_creditor: The person receiving the transferred property is not one of the debtor’s creditors.
predicates.transfer_not_voidable_solely_because_tra: The transfer is not voidable solely because the recipient is not a creditor.

issues.definition: When a creditor challenges a transfer, payment of genuine debts for adequate consideration without a retained benefit means that a non-creditor recipient’s status alone does not make the transfer voidable.

issues.legal_issue: In an appeal by special leave, factual challenges are not entertained unless material evidence was ignored or the finding under challenge was perverse.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the adequacy of the sale consideration and alleged that some discharged debts were owed to company directors.
The High Court had made no finding supporting those allegations.
The Supreme Court found no basis to conclude that material evidence had been ignored or that the High Court’s finding was perverse.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not permit the factual challenges to be raised because the required basis for disturbing the High Court’s findings was absent.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court will not permit questions of fact to be raised unless material evidence has been ignored by the High Court or its finding is perverse.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and factual_challenge and (material_evidence_ignored or finding_perverse)

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court by special leave.
predicates.factual_challenge: A party asks the Supreme Court to revisit a factual issue decided below.
predicates.material_evidence_ignored: The court below failed to consider material evidence relevant to the factual finding.
predicates.finding_perverse: The factual finding of the court below is perverse.
predicates.factual_challenge_may_be_considered: The Supreme Court may consider the factual challenge.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, a factual challenge may be considered when material evidence was ignored or the finding under challenge was perverse.
